headline: Build every list a parse or an encode reads from by defining its indexes, so an accessor inherited from the array prototype cannot take an element as it is added.
summary: Appending to an array with `push` stores at an index, and a store consults the prototype chain for a setter. An accessor installed at an array index therefore receives each element as it is appended, leaves the array no own property there, and the index then reads back whatever the accessor answers. Binding `push` at load does not change that: it fixes which function runs, not what the function does. Assigning at an index and prepending have the same shape. Measured, a SEQUENCE of the integers 1 and 2 decoded with its first value replaced; the INTEGER 128 encoded as 0; the identifier sha256WithRSAEncryption encoded as a different identifier; a SEQUENCE wrapping a 300-byte OCTET STRING encoded as an empty SEQUENCE; and an ACME challenge token carrying a character the base64url set does not allow was accepted. This release converts every list on a parse or an encode path, both codecs included, removes the prepending append from the library, and makes the character tables an allow-list check reads hold no prototype. The direct calls in the message builders and the reporting verbs have the same shape and are not converted yet.

Fixed: The DER codec encodes the bytes a value describes. Four of its byte lists were built by prepending or by assigning at an index, and both are stores: an accessor inherited at an array index took the octets as they were produced, and the decisions read back off those lists were then read through the hole a store leaves. Measured: `pki.asn1.build.integer(128n)` emitted the INTEGER 0, a nine-digit integer emitted as all zeroes, -300 emitted as +212, `pki.asn1.build.oid("1.2.840.113549.1.1.11")` emitted a different OBJECT IDENTIFIER, a SEQUENCE wrapping 300 bytes emitted as `3000`, and tag 31 emitted a truncated identifier. The length octets, the identifier octets and an INTEGER's content octets are written into the output directly now, and an OID's sub-identifier octets are appended by defining each index, so all four describe the value they encode.

A decoded value's children are appended by defining the index, in both codecs. Those children are what every format module reads its fields out of. On a SEQUENCE of the integers 1 and 2 the first value came back as 9, and a certificate parsed with the accessor's value in place of its first relative distinguished name, throwing a bare TypeError rather than a typed refusal. The segments a constructed string is joined from, an identifier's arcs, and the checked children of every constructed element are built the same way.

Every list the schema engine builds is appended to by defining its index. The engine walks each SEQUENCE OF and SET OF into the list a format's own reader takes its elements from, and collects a structure's fields into the list that is concatenated in order into the bytes it emits, so an accessor at an array index decided both what a parse bound and what an encode wrote. The elements are also mapped through an operation captured at load, which neither dispatches through a replaceable `map` nor builds its result through the receiver's `Symbol.species`.

The tables that decide whether a string is a token, a label, a decimal-digit string or a hexadecimal escape held an entry per character they allow and nothing at the codes they do not, and reading one at a code it had no entry for answered from the array prototype. A value installed at index 47 therefore made `pki.acme.keyAuthorization` accept a challenge token carrying `/`, which the base64url set does not allow, instead of refusing it with `acme/bad-token`. The tables have no prototype now, so there is nothing to inherit. The same helper in the name guard was already written this way.

The certificate-policy tree is read at the depth a node was placed at. The per-depth layers were held in an array, so a depth with no node yet was a hole and reading it answered from the array prototype, which handed the policy processing a layer of the caller's choosing along with the expected policy sets its nodes carry. Creating a layer was a store at the same index. The layers are keyed in a record with no prototype now, and a generated node takes a qualifier only from a list that holds one.

Removing a policy node constructs nothing. The removal went through `splice`, which returns what it removed and therefore builds that result through the receiver's construction protocol: it reads the list's `constructor` and then that constructor's `Symbol.species`, so an accessor installed on `Array.prototype.constructor` ran during the unlink with the live list of policy-node records as its subject, which is a window to change a surviving node's expected-policy set before the walk reads it. Binding `splice` at load does not close that lookup, because the lookup is part of what the function does. The removal now defines the surviving slots and returns nothing. The same change covers the certificate list `pki.cmp` reorders while it accumulates authenticated CA certificates, the extension list every certificate parse builds, and the key-usage list `pki.webcrypto` copies from a caller.

An extension or an attribute is found by searching, not by indexing a selection. Written as a filter whose first element is taken, the selection is an empty list when nothing matched, and reading index 0 of an empty list answers from the array prototype: a value installed there stood in for an extension or attribute the input does not carry, and the refusal that follows the lookup was not reached. That covers the subject key identifier a CMS signer is matched by, the message-digest attribute a countersignature and an authenticated-attribute set are checked against, the key usage that decides whether an issuer may sign a CRL, the acmeIdentifier and SubjectAltName extensions a TLS-ALPN validation certificate must carry, and the authority key identifier `pki.acme.ariCertId` reads.

Every list a parse builds is appended to by defining its index, across the certificate, CRL, CSR, PKCS#8, CMS, OCSP, TSP, CMP, CMC, PKCS#12, attribute-certificate, trust-anchor and C509 readers, the CBOR codec under C509, and the content-key recovery in `pki.cms.decrypt`, whose key-derivation input is assembled the same way. A SCEP response's certificates and CRLs are checked one at a time and collected the same way, so the certificate returned is the one the check accepted. The trust anchors a path is built against, the addresses a request is allowed to connect to, the anchors a handshake runs under, the distribution-point names a revocation check compares, and the RC2 key schedule a legacy PKCS#12 import derives are all built this way too.

The lists built outside the readers are appended to the same way: a certificate's extension rows in the CSR, CRL and CRMF readers, the byte strings an HPKE key schedule is computed over, the peer chain `pki.transport.peerChain` returns, and the lists `pki.acme`, `pki.cmp`, `pki.est`, `pki.ct`, `pki.tuf`, `pki.tlog`, `pki.jose`, `pki.webcrypto` and the PKCS#11 URI reader build while they work.

A transparency-log tile is requested from the path its index describes. The path segments were prepended into a list and the per-segment prefix was then applied by a read-modify-write through the hole a prepend leaves, so an accessor at an array index reduced `pki.tlog.tilePath(0, 1234067n)` to `tile/0/`.

A C509 iPAddress constraint carries the address it encodes. Its octets were prepended into a list whose leading entry is both the prefix length checked for range and a byte the result carries, so an accessor at an array index decided the check and the emitted address together.

A length-prefixed vector declares the bytes it writes. The wire writer under `pki.ct`'s signed-certificate-timestamp list measured the caller's view and then wrote from that same view, so a body on a resizable buffer could shrink in between: the frame then declared more bytes than it carried, and the concatenation that assembles the output failed with an error from the runtime rather than a verdict from the writer. A bound was also converted inside the comparison the length is checked by, which ran the bound's own conversion before the prefix was written and let it replace the write that states the length: measured, a vector declared a length of zero over a payload of two bytes. The body is copied into the writer's own allocation before it is measured, the bounds are converted and typed up front, and the writes that place an integer in its field are bound when the module loads.

Every component of the preimage `pki.ct.reconstructSignedData` rebuilds is appended by defining its index, and the concatenation is bound at load. Those bytes are what a log's signature is verified over, so an accessor inherited at an array index replacing any one of them, the version, the signature type, the timestamp, the entry type, the certificate or the extensions, would put the verification on bytes the log never signed.

The lists `pki.cms.sign` builds while it works are appended to by defining their indexes: a message's signed attributes, its certificate set and its signer infos, including a countersignature's own signing-time attribute, signed-attribute bytes, signature algorithm and signature as they are assembled into the SignerInfo that is then signed.
Changed: The library no longer has a storing append to reach for, and a check refuses one that is written anyway: a module that reads `push` or `unshift` off a prototype as a value, quotes either inside brackets, or binds either by a declared destructuring pattern fails the static gates with the non-storing form named in the message. Both grow the list, so both store at an index the array has no own property at; the mutators that remain move or drop elements that already have own slots and reach no inherited accessor. A module prepending to a list counts its elements and appends them in order instead. What the check cannot settle is a property reached without naming it, through a runtime-assembled key or reflection, and a pattern in a parameter list, which is written exactly as an object passed as an argument is. What the rest rests on is that neither name is captured or exported anywhere in the library, so there is nothing to bind by habit, and that the non-storing primitives carry the tests for the behavior.

The same check now recognizes the variable-width and 64-bit integer writes (`writeUIntBE` and its siblings) alongside the fixed-width ones it already knew, so a module that reads one of those off the prototype at the moment it writes a field is reported like any other.
